exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: May a sponsor board delegate routine grant approval to a version-pinned deterministic policy, and who is the fund manager for §4966/§4967?
original_provisional_answer: Build the deterministic approval tier. Until counsel and the sponsor board approve delegation, its outcome is 'ApproveRecommended', which a human approves in one-click batches (A4). After approval the same rule outcome becomes the A3 approval itself, with no code change, only an authority-flag change.
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC §4966) plus sponsor's state of incorporation (nonprofit corporation law)

authoritative_findings.claim: A fund manager is an officer, director or trustee of the sponsor (or person with similar powers) and, for any act or failure to act, an employee having authority or responsibility for it.
The 5% fund-manager tax applies only to a fund manager who agreed to the distribution knowing it was taxable; the 20% sponsor tax applies without a knowledge element.

Proposed rule (not effective, reliance permitted): a person delegated final authority by an officer/director/trustee or the governing body has officer-like authority and is a fund manager; a person merely implementing a superior's decision is not; 'agreement' is any manifestation of approval sufficient to exercise authority to approve or to recommend approval.
Proposed knowledge standard: no negligent failure to ascertain where the distributee is listed on Tax Exempt Organization Search as a §170(b)(1)(A) organization other than a supporting organization.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Preamble, fund manager discussion (88 FR 77933); Prop. §53.4966-2(c)(3)

authoritative_findings.claim: State corporate law example: business and affairs are managed by or under the direction of the board, which may designate committees exercising board powers.
No federal statute or regulation requires a human to approve each grant individually; the requirement is that the sponsor own and control the fund and have exclusive legal control.

supporting_interpretation: A board may adopt a versioned deterministic grant policy and delegate final approval authority for grants that satisfy it to a named officer or committee (or adopt it as a board/committee act). The rule engine is not a 'person'; fund-manager status attaches to the humans who hold the delegated authority (and to those who approve the policy or its exceptions). Because §4966 taxable-distribution status for routine grants to §170(b)(1)(A) recipients is avoided by the statutory exception, delegated automated approval for that class carries low tax exposure if eligibility data is reliable (TEOS reliance under Rev. Proc. 2018-32).
competing_interpretation: Some counsel may say each grant must have a documented human 'manifestation of approval' so that responsibility is identifiable, and that a standing delegation to a rule makes every member of the approving body a potential 'agreeing' fund manager for each rule output. Under the proposed rule's broad 'agreement' definition, approving the policy could be treated as agreement to each resulting distribution.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound supplies the rule engine; the sponsor supplies the authority. Unbound must record which named officer/committee holds the delegated authority for each policy version, so that the accountable fund managers are identifiable for Form 4720 purposes.
business_assumptions: Sponsor is a nonprofit corporation whose bylaws permit delegation to officers/committees
Automated tier limited to §170(b)(1)(A) non-supporting-organization recipients with TEOS/BMF evidence
AI never approves (CAP-41)
recommended_answer: Yes, with conditions. A board resolution (or bylaw-authorized committee act) may (1) adopt the version-pinned policy, (2) delegate final approval of grants that satisfy it to a named officer or committee, and (3) name who reviews exceptions. The fund managers for §4966/§4967 are the sponsor's officers, directors and trustees, plus the delegated officer/committee members and any employee with final authority over the act or failure to act. Keep the build as decided ('ApproveRecommended' until the authority flag is set), but the trigger to flip the flag is the board resolution, not a counsel opinion. Restrict auto-approval to §170(b)(1)(A) non-supporting-organization recipients verified on TEOS.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether the IRS would treat policy approval as 'agreement' to every resulting distribution (proposed rule only); state-specific limits on delegation for the sponsor's state; proposed rules not final.
consequences_if_wrong: If a taxable distribution occurs, the sponsor owes 20% regardless; delegated approvers could owe 5% (max $10,000 per distribution) if knowledge is shown. Governance criticism if delegation is not documented.
conservative_fallback: Human one-click batch approval of rule-recommended grants by a named delegated officer (A4), which still produces an identifiable 'agreeing' manager per batch.
alternative_design: Delegate to a named officer who approves rule outputs in daily batches with sampling (cost: minutes/day; friction: low; exposure: same as full automation but clearer accountability; lost opportunity: small latency). Versus full automation under board resolution (lowest cost; same tax exposure for exempt classes; needs documented delegation).
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a policy version without a recorded board resolution reference and delegate, When the rule outputs Approve, Then the outcome is ApproveRecommended and requires human approval.
Given a recorded board resolution delegating authority to officer X for policy version V, When a grant satisfies V, Then the approval record names X as accountable approver and V as the authority.
Given a recipient not listed on TEOS as §170(b)(1)(A) (or a supporting organization), When evaluated, Then automated approval is unavailable.
Given any grant, When approved, Then the record retains the identity of every person holding approval authority for Form 4720 fund-manager reporting.
reconsideration_triggers: Final §4966 regulations or withdrawal of REG-142338-07
IRS guidance on automated grant approval
Any incident where an auto-approved grant is a taxable distribution
external_authorization_required: Sponsor board resolution (or bylaw-authorized committee resolution) adopting the versioned grant policy and delegating final approval authority to named officer(s)/committee, recorded with effective dates.

corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: RCD-005 (decisions.csv) validation_required 'Counsel Q1 + sponsor board resolution'
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Treats a counsel opinion as a legal precondition; no statute or regulation requires one.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: The legally necessary authorization is the board (or committee) delegation; counsel review is optional assurance. Fund manager definition is established by §4966(d)(3).

landscape_update_candidates: Proposed §53.4966-1(i)(2) delegation rule and §53.4966-2(c)(3) TEOS-based knowledge safe harbor are relevant to sponsor automation benchmarking.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: What do grant-recipient classes, related-party payee blocks and expenditure responsibility require?
original_provisional_answer: Release 1 permits grants only to excepted recipients (see RCD-013), with a donor-control certification for supporting organizations and the related-party payee block always on. Expenditure-responsibility, private-foundation, non-functionally-integrated Type III, foreign and individual recipients are rejected with an explanation.

authoritative_findings.claim: Any DAF distribution to a natural person is a taxable distribution; no expenditure-responsibility cure exists for natural persons.
Distributions to other persons are taxable unless for a §170(c)(2)(B) purpose and the sponsor exercises expenditure responsibility under §4945(h).
Not taxable: distributions to §170(b)(1)(A) organizations other than disqualified supporting organizations, to the sponsor, or to another DAF.
Disqualified supporting organizations: non-functionally-integrated Type III, and other supporting organizations whose supported organization is controlled by the donor/advisor and related persons.
Private operating foundations and certain conduit foundations are §170(b)(1)(A)(vii) organizations, so DAF grants to them fall within the statutory exception.
Any grant, loan, compensation or similar payment from a DAF to a donor, donor-advisor, family member (incl. siblings) or 35%-controlled entity is an excess benefit in full.

ER requires pre-grant inquiry, signed grantee commitment (repay unused funds, annual reports, records, no lobbying/electioneering/non-charitable use), reports; the proposed rule substitutes no grants to natural persons or to donors/related persons.
Grantors may rely on TEOS/EO BMF public-charity classification (including for §4966 grants) absent knowledge or responsibility.

supporting_interpretation: The provisional decision is a lawful product scope narrower than the law. Unsupported classes (ER grants, non-operating private foundations, NFI Type III, foreign without ED, individuals) are not prohibited by law except grants to natural persons, which are always taxable.
competing_interpretation: Some sponsors (e.g., Fidelity Charitable) treat private operating foundations and governmental units as eligible; excluding them may lose demand. Foreign grantees with a current ED are treated as §170(b)(1)(A) under existing guidance.
applicability_to_unbound: Recipient-class engine must distinguish 'unsupported by product' from 'taxable by statute' in explanations.
business_assumptions: Release 1 has no ER workflow
Donor-control certification captured at recommendation time
recommended_answer: Confirm the release-1 scope with three corrections: (1) label private operating foundations and §170(b)(1)(F) conduit foundations as 'legally excepted, unsupported in R1' rather than as ER-required private foundations; (2) governmental units (§170(c)(1)) for exclusively public purposes are excepted and may be enabled by sponsor policy; (3) only natural-person grants are taxable without cure, so the rejection explanation for other classes must say 'not supported by this sponsor/release', not 'prohibited by law'. Keep the related-party payee block always on (§4958(c)(2) is automatic, whole-amount). Keep the supporting-organization donor-control certification.
remaining_uncertainty: Product demand for ER/foreign classes; proposed-rule details on supporting organization certifications are not final. No statute or proposed rule provides a donor-certification safe harbor for supporting-organization control; the certification is a sponsor evidence practice (the proposed certification rule in Prop. §53.4966-4(a)(4)(ii) concerns single-identified-organization funds).
consequences_if_wrong: Mis-labeling causes donor confusion; enabling unsupported classes without ER would create 20% sponsor tax.
alternative_design: Route excluded classes to a partner sponsor or a domestic intermediary (catalogued) instead of rejecting outright: low cost, retains donor intent, no ER burden.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a recipient that is a natural person, When a grant is recommended, Then it is rejected with reason STATUTORY_NATURAL_PERSON.
Given a private operating foundation, When recommended in R1, Then the explanation states 'legally excepted under §170(b)(1)(A)(vii); not supported in release 1'.
Given a Type I/II supporting organization, When recommended without donor-control certification, Then the grant is held.
Given a payee matching a donor, advisor, family member (incl. siblings) or 35% entity, When evaluated, Then the grant is blocked.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Private operating foundations and §170(b)(1)(F)(ii)/(iii) foundations are §170(b)(1)(A)(vii) organizations and excepted from §4966 taxable distributions; only non-operating private foundations need ER.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: §4966 does not prohibit; it taxes. Only natural-person distributions are taxable without cure.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Describe as excise-tax exposure and product scope.

landscape_update_candidates: Fidelity Charitable 2026 guidelines: private operating foundations and §170(c)(1) governmental units eligible; foreign charities generally not; good standing under federal and state law required.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Pledges: platform-wide prohibition or sponsor policy under Notice 2017-73?
original_provisional_answer: Pledge handling is sponsor policy. Platform default is 'NoticeConditions' (grants that satisfy Notice 2017-73 are allowed; the sponsor never references the pledge; remittance metadata strips pledge references). Sponsors may choose 'Prohibited'.

authoritative_findings.claim: Treasury/IRS stated that a DAF distribution to a charity to which a donor/advisor has pledged (enforceable or not) would not be a more-than-incidental §4967 benefit if (1) the sponsor makes no reference to the pledge, (2) no other more-than-incidental benefit, (3) no deduction claimed for the distribution.
'Taxpayers may rely on the rules described in section 4 until additional guidance is issued.'
The rule applies for §4967 only.

The 2023 NPRM only recites Notice 2017-73 as background and does not finalize or withdraw the pledge rule; no final §4966/§4967 regulations or withdrawal appear in the Federal Register as of 2026-11-24.
2026-27 Priority Guidance Plan lists further guidance on certain DAF arrangements without timetable.
Fidelity Charitable permits grants satisfying non-legally binding pledges but not enforceable pledges.

supporting_interpretation: Notice 2017-73 §4 remains current reliance guidance; 'additional guidance' has not been issued. A sponsor following the three conditions has a reliance position on §4967. Because the proposed §4966 rule would make any use conferring more-than-incidental benefit a deemed distribution, the Notice conditions also limit that (proposed) exposure.
competing_interpretation: Conservative sponsors restrict to non-binding pledges because paying an enforceable personal obligation is a classic self-dealing benefit in the private-foundation context, and the Notice describes regulations under consideration rather than final law.
applicability_to_unbound: Platform must support three sponsor policy values and suppress pledge references in all sponsor-issued artifacts; the third condition (no deduction) is the donor's obligation, supported by remittance and summary language.
business_assumptions: Sponsors differ in risk appetite
Recipients may still record the grant against a pledge internally
recommended_answer: Pledge handling remains a sponsor policy (Prohibited / NonBindingOnly / NoticeConditions). Notice 2017-73 §7 reliance is verified as still in effect (no superseding guidance as of 2026-11-24), so NoticeConditions is a lawful option. Platform default at onboarding: require the sponsor to choose explicitly; if a default is needed, use NonBindingOnly (market-leader practice, low friction), with NoticeConditions selectable. The reviewed answer's 'prohibit until reliance verified' is resolved: reliance is verified.
remaining_uncertainty: Future §4967 proposed regulations could change conditions; reliance ends when additional guidance is issued.
consequences_if_wrong: 125% §4967 tax on advisor/recipient and 10% on knowing managers if a distribution is held to confer more-than-incidental benefit.
alternative_design: Never accept pledge data at all (no capture): avoids reference risk but loses donor convenience and recipient matching; versus capturing pledge data internally with outbound suppression (current design).
required_acceptance_criteria: Given policy NoticeConditions and a recommendation flagged as pledge payment, When the grant is remitted, Then no outbound artifact (check memo, ACH addenda, remittance, portal, webhook) contains pledge identifiers or vocabulary.
Given any pledge-flagged grant, When evaluated, Then the other-benefit gate runs and the donor summary states no deduction may be claimed for the distribution.
Given IRS publishes guidance superseding Notice 2017-73 §4, When recorded in the watch list, Then pledge policy NoticeConditions is suspended pending review.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Required default prohibition until reliance guidance verified.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Reliance verified 2026-11-24: Notice 2017-73 §7 reliance continues; no superseding guidance published.

landscape_update_candidates: Fidelity Charitable: non-binding pledges only (help text).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Advisor compensation from fund assets and the §4958 / proposed-regulation exposure.
original_provisional_answer: Release 1 does not pay advisors with a personal relationship to the donor from DAF assets. Investment managers engaged by the sponsor under sponsor contract are allowed. Watch item on REG-142338-07.

authoritative_findings.claim: A donor-advisor includes any person appointed or designated by the donor who has or expects advisory privileges over the distribution or investment of amounts in the fund.

Any compensation or similar payment from a DAF to a §4958(f)(7) person (donor, donor-advisor, family, 35% entity) is an excess benefit transaction in its entire amount; 25% tax on recipient, 10% on knowing managers.
Investment advisors compensated by the sponsor for managing DAF assets are disqualified persons with respect to the sponsor (ordinary excess-over-value test).

Proposed rule: a §4958(f)(8)(B) investment advisor managing both the DAF and the donor's personal assets is a donor-advisor while in that dual capacity, whether or not appointed by the donor, unless properly viewed as serving the sponsor as a whole (e.g., fees charged uniformly across all DAFs).
REG-142338-07 is neither finalized nor withdrawn as of 2026-11-24; PGP 2026-27 lists guidance on certain DAF arrangements.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Federal Register search; EV-A-011 EO item 4

supporting_interpretation: The exposure is not only proposed-regulation exposure: under the statute, an advisor the donor designates with investment advisory privileges over the fund is a donor-advisor, so any compensation paid from that fund to the advisor is an automatic excess benefit. Sponsor-engaged managers paid under a sponsor program with uniform fee terms, who hold no donor-designated advisory privilege, fall under ordinary §4958 reasonableness.
competing_interpretation: Industry advisor-managed DAF programs treat the advisor as the sponsor's engaged manager even when the donor recommended them; commenters argued regulated advisors pose little risk. Until final rules, many sponsors continue paying such advisors from fund assets.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound must classify the advisor-fund relationship and block fee accrual where the payee is a donor-advisor of that fund.
business_assumptions: Release 1 has no advisor-managed DAF program
Sponsor contracts directly with any investment manager
recommended_answer: Keep the release-1 block, restated: no compensation from a fund to any person who is a donor-advisor of that fund under §4966(d)(2)(A)(iii) (including an advisor the donor designated with investment privileges) or to the donor's family/35% entities. Allow sponsor-engaged managers whose fees are set by sponsor contract and charged uniformly or ratably across a program and who were not designated by the donor for that fund. Treat the dual-capacity 'personal investment advisor' rule as a reliance-eligible proposal that sponsors may choose to follow; keep REG-142338-07 on the watch list.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether a donor 'recommendation' of an advisor who is then engaged by the sponsor counts as 'appointed or designated'; final rule content.
consequences_if_wrong: Full amount of fees is an excess benefit (25% on advisor, 200% second tier if uncorrected; 10% on knowing managers); correction cannot be repaid into any DAF.
conservative_fallback: No advisor compensation from DAF assets at all in release 1; investment management only through sponsor-wide pools.
alternative_design: Sponsor-level pools with a single sponsor-paid manager (fee in NAV), donors choose pools only: no advisor fees from individual funds; lost opportunity: advisor-channel distribution.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an advisor recorded as designated by the donor with investment privileges for fund F, When a fee accrual from F to that advisor is attempted, Then it is blocked with reason DONOR_ADVISOR_COMPENSATION.
Given a sponsor-contracted manager with a uniform program fee schedule and no donor designation, When fees accrue, Then accrual proceeds and the classification record is cited.
Given final §4966 regulations are published, When recorded, Then all advisor classifications are queued for review.
reconsideration_triggers: New PGP guidance on DAF arrangements
external_authorization_required: Executed sponsor investment-management agreement stating the manager serves the sponsor's program as a whole, with fee terms uniform across participating funds.

corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: RCD-021 decision_basis 'Conservative pending §4958 and proposed-regulation analysis'
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Frames exposure as arising mainly from proposed regulations.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Statute already makes donor-designated advisors with investment privileges donor-advisors (§4966(d)(2)(A)(iii)); compensation to them from the fund is an automatic excess benefit under §4958(c)(2).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Tax-fit guidance and donor annual summaries.
original_provisional_answer: No individualized tax advice. Donor summaries and assistant answers use counsel-approved disclosures, including that DAF contributions do not qualify for the nonitemizer deduction (IR-2026-135). Bunching calculators are excluded from release 1.
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC §170); state law on professional advice not researched

authoritative_findings.claim: Nonitemizer deduction excludes contributions to supporting organizations and for establishing or maintaining a DAF.
IRS: 'Cash contributions made either to supporting organizations or to establish or maintain a donor advised fund do not qualify.'
Itemized charitable deductions are allowed only above 0.5% of the contribution base (taxable years after 2025).
A DAF contribution deduction requires a contemporaneous written acknowledgment that the sponsor has exclusive legal control over the contributed assets.
No federal rule prohibits a charity from giving general, non-individualized tax information; whether individualized output is 'advice' is a liability and conflict question.

supporting_interpretation: General educational content and statutory facts (nonitemizer exclusion, 0.5% floor, acknowledgment content) can be stated without counsel because they restate statute and IRS releases. Personalized projections (bunching calculators) would apply law to the donor's facts and create reliance and conflict risk for a sponsor that benefits from contributions.
competing_interpretation: Many sponsors publish bunching illustrations; a calculator using user-entered hypothetical inputs with clear disclaimers is generally treated as education, not advice.
applicability_to_unbound: Donor summaries and assistant answers can quote approved statements built from statute/IRS text; versioned by tax year.
business_assumptions: Sponsor does not employ credentialed tax preparers for donors
Assistant answers are reviewed templates
recommended_answer: Confirm: no individualized tax advice. Disclosure text can be built directly from verified authority without paid review: (a) DAF contributions do not qualify for the §170(p) nonitemizer deduction (IR-2026-135); (b) itemized charitable deductions are subject to a 0.5% floor from 2026; (c) the acknowledgment states the sponsor's exclusive legal control and whether goods or services were provided; (d) grants from the fund are not deductible by the donor. Bunching calculators remain excluded from R1 as a business decision; a generic illustration with fixed hypothetical numbers is a lower-risk alternative.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether the sponsor's counsel wants extra disclaimers; tax-year changes.
consequences_if_wrong: Donor reliance claims and reputational harm if summaries misstate deductibility.
conservative_fallback: Statute-quoted disclosures only; link to IRS Publication 526/6196.
alternative_design: Static, fixed-number illustration instead of interactive calculator: low cost, minimal reliance risk, retains educational value.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a donor annual summary for tax year 2026+, When generated, Then it contains the approved nonitemizer-exclusion statement and the 0.5% floor statement versioned to the tax year.
Given an assistant question asking how much the donor will save, When answered, Then the assistant gives general rules and declines a personalized computation.
Given a DAF contribution acknowledgment, When issued, Then it states exclusive legal control per §170(f)(18).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Is a complex-asset intermediary an agent of the sponsor or the donee?
original_provisional_answer: Donee model for release 1: the intermediary charity is donee of record; it acknowledges the asset and handles 8283/8282 and §4943; the DAF later receives cash from it.

authoritative_findings.claim: The donee organization that received the property signs Form 8283 Section B Part V.
Donee organizations report dispositions within three years on Form 8282.
A deduction for a contribution to a DAF requires the sponsor's written acknowledgment of exclusive legal control.
IRS position: a donation to a US charity that is merely a conduit or is earmarked for another recipient is treated by reference to the ultimate recipient.
Rev. Rul. 63-252 conduit principle: control and discretion of the intermediate charity determine the true donee.
Market example: Fidelity Charitable receives complex assets itself and allocates review, holding and sale costs to the giving account (sponsor-as-donee with service providers).

supporting_interpretation: If the intermediary is contractually bound to sell the asset and remit proceeds for credit to the donor's DAF, it is acting as a conduit, so the sponsor is likely the true donee. Then the sponsor (not the intermediary) must give the §170(f)(18) acknowledgment, sign Form 8283 Part V and file Form 8282, and the DAF holds the asset for §4943 purposes. A genuine donee model requires the intermediary to have discretion over the proceeds, which defeats the donor's expectation of DAF credit and makes the later transfer the intermediary's own grant.
competing_interpretation: Some practitioners use an affiliated charity or supporting organization as donee that later makes a discretionary grant to the sponsor; when that charity is a separate public charity with real discretion, it is the donee and the donor's deduction is for a gift to it, not to the DAF.
applicability_to_unbound: The intermediary-agreement record must capture which entity has legal control, and the donor-facing acknowledgment must come from that entity.
business_assumptions: Release 1 does not hold complex assets
Donors expect DAF credit for complex-asset gifts
recommended_answer: Do not rely on the 'donee model' as a way to keep tax duties out of release 1 when the donor expects DAF credit. Use the agent model: the sponsor is donee of record (acknowledgment, Form 8283 Part V, Form 8282, §4943 holding) and the intermediary or vendor is the sponsor's contracted agent for receipt, custody and sale. Allow the donee model only where the intermediary agreement gives the intermediary discretion over proceeds and the donor is told the deduction is for a gift to the intermediary, with any later transfer to the sponsor being the intermediary's grant. If neither is acceptable for R1, exclude complex assets from R1.
remaining_uncertainty: Rev. Rul. 63-252 full text not fetched; no authority addresses DAF complex-asset intermediaries directly; §4943(e) application not verified in this pass.
consequences_if_wrong: Donor deduction denied for lack of a valid §170(f)(18) acknowledgment from the true donee; missing 8283/8282 filings; penalties; reputational harm.
alternative_design: Agent model with a specialist vendor under sponsor contract (fee per transaction charged to the fund as a disclosed cost): moderate cost, sponsor bears filings, preserves complex-asset demand.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an intermediary agreement without a recorded legal-control structure, When a complex-asset gift is initiated, Then the workflow is blocked.
Given agent model, When the asset is received, Then the sponsor issues the acknowledgment and the Form 8283 Part V signing task is assigned to the sponsor's authorized signer.
Given donee model, When the donor confirms, Then the donor-facing text states the gift is to the intermediary and DAF credit is not guaranteed.
reconsideration_triggers: Counsel or IRS guidance on DAF intermediaries
external_authorization_required: Executed intermediary/vendor agreement stating which entity takes legal title and control (agent agreement for the agent model).

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Assumes the donee model keeps 8283/8282/§4943 duties out of release 1 while the DAF later receives the cash.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: If the intermediary is bound to pass proceeds to the donor's DAF, the conduit doctrine and §170(f)(18) point to the sponsor as donee. The donee model works only with real intermediary discretion.

landscape_update_candidates: Fidelity Charitable allocates complex-asset review, holding and sale costs to the giving account (net proceeds model).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: May a sponsor rely on ED written advice procured by another grantor or an ED repository, and on what contractual terms?
original_provisional_answer: A sponsor may rely on equivalency-determination written advice obtained through a repository or another grantor when the advice is current under Rev. Proc. 2017-53 §3.03(1), the practitioner or repository authorizes reliance by the sponsor in writing, and the sponsor has no contrary knowledge. Expiry is computed from the grantee's taxable year.

authoritative_findings.claim: A determination is ordinarily in good faith if based on current written advice received from a qualified tax practitioner (attorney, CPA, enrolled agent under Circular 230) and reasonably relied on per §1.6664-4(c)(1).
Currency: law unchanged since the advice and facts from the grantee's current or prior taxable year; public-support advice current for two grantee taxable years after the five-year test period.

Shared advice from another foundation may be used if reasonable under all facts and circumstances, but for the special rule the advice must be received from the qualified tax practitioner rather than from another foundation.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: 80 FR 57713-57714 'Reliance on Written Advice Shared by Another Foundation'

authoritative_findings.claim: DAF sponsors may use the ED guidelines/regulations pending further guidance.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Rev. Proc. 2017-53 §2; EV-A-014 preamble and fn 4

authoritative_findings.claim: NGOsource's on-file badge reflects a determination for a specific funder during a specific period (search snippet only).

supporting_interpretation: The decision is mostly right but the reliance condition must be tightened: to get the 'ordinarily good faith' special rule, the sponsor must receive the written advice from the qualified tax practitioner (for example a practitioner letter addressed to or extending reliance to the sponsor, as repository models do per subscriber). Authorization by a non-practitioner repository or forwarding by another grantor gives only the general facts-and-circumstances standard.
competing_interpretation: A sponsor could rely on shared advice under the general good-faith rule when it knows the practitioner and the sharing grantor's diligence (TD 9740 preamble example).
applicability_to_unbound: EquivalencyDetermination record must distinguish 'received from practitioner' versus 'shared by grantor/repository' and route the latter to sponsor review.
business_assumptions: Sponsors subscribe to a repository whose practitioners issue advice per subscriber
recommended_answer: Revise: the routine (non-ER) path is allowed only when the sponsor has current written advice received from a qualified tax practitioner (directly or via a repository whose practitioner issues the advice or an express reliance letter to the sponsor), no contrary knowledge, and currency computed per §53.4945-5(a)(5). Advice merely forwarded by another grantor or authorized only by a non-practitioner repository goes to sponsor review under the general good-faith standard, not the automatic path. Currency is computed from the grantee's taxable year.
remaining_uncertainty: Exact contractual form of repository reliance (not verified by fetch); final §4966 rules might change details.
consequences_if_wrong: Grant treated as to a non-§170(b)(1)(A) organization without ER: 20% sponsor tax, 5% knowing managers.
alternative_design: Use a domestic intermediary (catalogued) for foreign grantees lacking practitioner-issued advice: no ED cost; donor intent preserved via non-binding preference.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an ED whose source is 'shared by another grantor' without practitioner-issued reliance to the sponsor, When approval is requested, Then the routine path is refused and a SponsorReview task is created.
Given practitioner advice issued to the sponsor dated 2026-03-01 based on FY2025 calendar-year data, When release occurs 2027-12-30, Then release proceeds; on 2028-01-02 it is held ED_EXPIRED.
Given a practitioner type outside attorney/CPA/enrolled agent, When approval is requested, Then it is rejected.
external_authorization_required: Repository subscription contract under which a qualified tax practitioner issues the written advice (or a reliance letter) to the sponsor.

related_question_answers.answer: Store provenance, scope, currency and reliance rights. Automatic reliance only on advice received from a qualified tax practitioner (directly or via a repository's practitioner-issued advice/reliance letter). Shared advice goes to review under the general good-faith standard (TD 9740 preamble).

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Allows reliance when 'the practitioner or repository authorizes reliance'.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: For the special rule the advice must be received from the qualified tax practitioner; repository-only authorization does not suffice (80 FR 57714).

landscape_update_candidates: TD 9740 preamble on shared advice is the key authority for ED repository economics.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: What purpose wording to an intermediary avoids an impermissible earmark for DAF grants?
original_provisional_answer: Grants to US intermediaries may carry a non-binding preference ('to support [intermediary]'s work in [country/program]'). They may never name a specific foreign grantee as a required recipient or require pass-through. The intermediary must retain discretion and control. Wording is catalogued per intermediary.

authoritative_findings.claim: Private-foundation analogue: a grant used by the grantee to pay a secondary grantee is not a grant to the secondary grantee if the grantor does not earmark it for a named secondary grantee and has no oral or written agreement to cause the selection; reason to believe is fine if the grantee controls selection independently.
Proposed anti-abuse rule: a series of distributions through intermediaries under a plan inconsistent with §4966 is treated as a single distribution.
Schedule F Part II includes grants to a domestic organization for the purpose of providing grants to a designated foreign organization.
Earmarked or conduit gifts are treated by reference to the ultimate recipient (IRS info letter; Rev. Rul. 63-252 principle).
Market practice: non-binding 'special purpose' designations conveyed to the recipient, which the sponsor may modify.

supporting_interpretation: Non-binding preferences for the intermediary's own program in a country or cause, with the intermediary retaining discretion and control, are consistent with the §53.4945-5(a)(6) analogue. Naming a specific foreign grantee (even as a preference) risks being an earmark for a named secondary grantee.
competing_interpretation: Some intermediaries (e.g., 'friends of' organizations) accept donor-advised recommendations of specific foreign grantees and run their own ED/ER; with genuine intermediary discretion this is defensible but depends on facts.
applicability_to_unbound: Catalogue wording and capture donor intent separately (internal evidence) from outbound wording.
business_assumptions: Intermediaries are §170(b)(1)(A) organizations with their own foreign grant programs
recommended_answer: Confirm the decision with one clarification: outbound wording may name the intermediary's program, country or cause; it must not name any specific foreign organization, even as a non-binding suggestion, and no side agreement may let the donor or sponsor cause selection. Donor's original foreign recommendation is retained only as internal evidence. Report as a domestic grant; the intermediary handles Schedule F for its grants.
remaining_uncertainty: No final §4966 earmark rule; PF analogue applied by interpretation.
consequences_if_wrong: Grant treated as made to the foreign organization: taxable distribution unless ED or ER (20%/5%).
alternative_design: Offer intermediary 'country funds' as catalogue items (pooled programs) so donors choose a program, not a grantee: low friction, low earmark risk.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given outbound purpose text containing the name of a foreign organization, When remittance is generated, Then it is blocked EARMARK_NAMED_SECONDARY_GRANTEE.
Given an accepted intermediary alternative, When remitted, Then purpose text equals the catalogue's approved wording and the donor's foreign recommendation is stored internally only.
reconsideration_triggers: Final §4966 regulations with an intermediary rule
IRS guidance on DAF grants via intermediaries

related_question_answers.answer: A suggestion of a specific foreign grantee is risky even when non-binding (PF analogue §53.4945-5(a)(6)(i) refers to earmarking for 'any named secondary grantee'). Capture discretion and suggestion separately; never transmit a named foreign grantee; route ambiguous restrictions to review.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Payee substitution to a merger successor: donor reconfirmation required?
original_provisional_answer: When a grantee merges, a legal successor with the same charitable purpose and an eligible status may receive open and recurring grants with sponsor approval and notice to the donor (no reconfirmation). If the purpose or recipient class changes, or the successor is not eligible, the grant is cancelled and the donor asked to re-recommend.
jurisdiction: US federal; state nonprofit merger law (not researched)

authoritative_findings.claim: The sponsor owns and controls DAF assets; donors hold only advisory privileges; contribution deduction depends on the sponsor's exclusive legal control.
TEOS/BMF reliance applies only to an organization listed under its official or recognized name and not before it is listed.
Proposed rule analogue: a single-identified-organization fund may substitute another organization upon reorganization that ends the named organization, if beyond donor control.
Market: donors have no legally enforceable right to any recommended grant; sponsor may decline.

supporting_interpretation: No federal rule requires donor reconfirmation; the sponsor makes the grant. The legal requirement is that the successor itself be an eligible recipient verified on its own EIN.
competing_interpretation: Donor-relations and state AG donor-intent norms favor reconfirmation where the successor's program differs; some sponsors reconfirm all substitutions.
applicability_to_unbound: Implement as sponsor policy with independent eligibility evaluation of the successor.
business_assumptions: Successor's charitable purpose can be compared from filings
recommended_answer: Confirm as a sponsor policy: substitution to a verified legal successor that independently passes eligibility (own EIN, TEOS listing, same recipient class) with sponsor approval and donor notice; recurring grants should carry a notice-and-opt-out window before the next disbursement. Reconfirm when purpose, class or eligibility changes.
remaining_uncertainty: State merger-law treatment of restricted gifts to constituent corporations not verified.
consequences_if_wrong: Donor complaints; possible grant to an ineligible successor if verification is skipped.
alternative_design: Cancel and auto-propose a re-recommendation pre-filled with the successor: one-click donor action, no unilateral substitution.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a MergerIntoSuccessor event, When open grants exist, Then grants are held until the successor passes eligibility on its own EIN and the sponsor approves.
Given approval, When a recurring grant next disburses, Then the donor has received notice at least N days earlier (sponsor-configured) with an opt-out.

related_question_answers.answer: Permitted without reconfirmation under federal law; verify legal succession and the successor's own eligibility; sponsor policy decides notice versus reconfirmation.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Is a §4966 taxable distribution correctable, and what is the incident reporting channel (Form 4720) for sponsor and managers?
original_provisional_answer: §4966 and §4967 first-tier taxes are 'qualified first tier taxes' under §4962 (subchapter G), so they are abatable if the event was due to reasonable cause, not wilful neglect, and is corrected within the correction period. The incident workflow therefore records reasonable-cause evidence and correction steps for every incident. Excise taxes are reported on Form 4720 by each liable person (sponsor; fund manager; donor/advisor for §4967). §4958 excess benefit is corrected within the correction period and also reported on Schedule L.

authoritative_findings.claim: Qualified first tier taxes include any first tier tax imposed by subchapter G (added 2007); subchapter G is §§4966-4967.
§§4966 and 4967 are first tier taxes and taxable events.
Abatement requires the Secretary to be satisfied of reasonable cause, no willful neglect, and correction within the correction period.

No second tier tax exists for §§4966/4967, 'correct' is defined by the section imposing the second tier tax, and the correction period ends by reference to a second-tier deficiency notice, extended by periods the Secretary finds reasonable.
IRS: use Form 843 to request abatement under §4962 of first tier taxes under §§4942-4945, 4955, 4958, 4966 and 4967.

Sponsor reports §4966 on Form 4720 Schedule K; fund managers and donors/advisors/related persons liable under §4967 file their own Form 4720 (Schedule L); §4958 is Schedule I; due 15th day of 5th month.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Who Must File; Schedules I, K, L

authoritative_findings.claim: Correction of a §4958(c)(2) DAF excess benefit may not be repaid into any DAF.

supporting_interpretation: Abatement is statutorily available for §4966 and §4967 first tier taxes, but 'correction' is undefined for them; in practice correction would mean recovering the amount and restoring it to charitable use, with the IRS setting the period. Abatement is discretionary and requested on Form 843.
competing_interpretation: Because there is no second tier tax or statutory correction definition, the IRS could find no correction mechanism and deny abatement except on its own terms.
applicability_to_unbound: Incident workflow records reasonable-cause evidence, recovery steps, and Form 4720/843 filing inputs for each liable person; it must not show liability as extinguished.
business_assumptions: Sponsor CPA prepares Form 4720
recommended_answer: The original answer is legally supported (abatement is available under §4962 for §4966/§4967 first tier taxes), and the review answer 'do not assert abatement' is too cautious. State it as: abatement may be requested on Form 843; it is discretionary and requires reasonable cause, no willful neglect, and correction, which is undefined for these taxes. Record recovery (repayment to the sponsor, not into any DAF for §4958(c)(2) cases), reasonable-cause evidence, and filing inputs: sponsor Form 4720 Schedule K; fund managers Schedule K Part II/L Part III; donors/advisors Schedule L; §4958 on Form 4720 Schedule I and Form 990 Schedule L Part I.
remaining_uncertainty: Meaning of 'correct' and the correction period end for §§4966/4967; IRS discretion.
consequences_if_wrong: Liability not abated; penalties for non-filing if Form 4720 is missed.
conservative_fallback: Treat taxes as owed; pursue abatement as a claim.
alternative_design: Pre-disbursement controls (eligibility gates) reduce incidence; incident workflow remains for residual cases.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an ExciseTaxIncident for §4966, When opened, Then filing inputs list Form 4720 Schedule K for the sponsor and each approving fund manager, and a Form 843 abatement task with reasonable-cause and correction evidence fields.
Given a §4958(c)(2) incident, When repayment is recorded, Then the repayment destination cannot be any DAF.
Given an incident, When displayed, Then status never shows 'abated' unless an IRS determination is recorded.
reconsideration_triggers: IRS guidance on §4962 for DAF taxes

related_question_answers.answer: Yes, §4962 abatement extends to §4966/§4967 first tier taxes (subchapter G), requested on Form 843; unlike §4958 there is no statutory correction definition, so record recovery and reasonable-cause evidence and do not show relief until the IRS grants it.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: 'Do not assert section 4962 abatement' contradicts §4962(b) and the Form 4720 instructions.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Abatement is available but discretionary; correction undefined.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: '§4958 ... also reported on Schedule L' is ambiguous: Form 4720 Schedule L is §4967.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: §4958 tax is on Form 4720 Schedule I; the transaction is disclosed on Form 990 Schedule L Part I.
Replace with 26 U.S.C. §§4962(b), 4963 and Form 4720 instructions (EV-A-003, -004, -017).

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: May a charity that holds an organization-advised fund recommend grants to itself?
original_provisional_answer: A fund established by a charity naming itself as beneficiary is classified as a designated/agency fund, not a DAF, and distributions to that charity follow the agency terms. If an organization-advised fund qualifies as a DAF, grants to the advising organization are permitted when it is a §170(b)(1)(A) organization (not a disqualified supporting organization), with the affiliation recorded and no benefit to any individual.

authoritative_findings.claim: A fund that makes distributions only to a single identified organization is not a DAF.
Distributions from a DAF to a §170(b)(1)(A) organization (not a disqualified SO) are not taxable distributions.
Any grant from a DAF to a donor or donor-advisor of that fund is an excess benefit in full; the statute does not exclude charities from 'donor'.

If the fund is a DAF (for example a private foundation or disqualified SO is the advisor, or the sponsor does not rely on the proposed rule), a grant to the advising organization fits the §4966 exception but is literally a grant to a 'donor' under §4958(c)(2).

applicability_to_unbound: Account-type classification must record the contributor/advisor type and the sponsor's choice to rely on the proposed definition.
business_assumptions: Most organization-advised funds at community foundations are agency or designated funds
recommended_answer: Revise: (1) a fund whose only beneficiary is the contributing charity is a single-identified-organization (designated/agency) fund, not a DAF, if distributions go only to that charity for its own activities; (2) a fund contributed and advised only by non-disqualified public charities may be classified as not a DAF in reliance on the proposed definition (sponsor policy choice, recorded); (3) where a fund is a DAF and the advising organization is a donor/advisor, block grants to that organization or its controlled entities (§4958(c)(2)), even if it is §170(b)(1)(A). No automatic self-grant approval.
remaining_uncertainty: Proposed rule not final; whether the IRS would apply §4958(c)(2) to a public-charity donor under current law is untested.
consequences_if_wrong: Full grant amount as excess benefit (25% on the recipient charity; 10% on knowing managers).
conservative_fallback: Classify all charity-advised funds as non-DAF agency/designated funds with single beneficiary, or bar charities as advisors (Fidelity practice).
alternative_design: Offer charities an agency/designated fund product instead of advisory privileges: avoids DAF classification entirely; loses flexible grantmaking for the charity.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a fund whose advisory-privilege holder is a public charity and whose classification is DAF, When a grant to that charity is recommended, Then it is blocked DONOR_IS_PAYEE.

Given a fund classified non-DAF under the sponsor's recorded reliance on the proposed definition, When a grant to the advising charity is recommended, Then fund-agreement rules apply and the classification basis is cited.
external_authorization_required: Sponsor board-approved account-type classification policy recording whether it relies on the proposed donor definition.

related_question_answers.answer: Not automatically. If the fund is a DAF, a grant to the advising organization is a §4958(c)(2) grant to a donor (block). If the fund is a single-beneficiary or public-charity-only fund (non-DAF under the proposed definition, reliance permitted), grants follow the fund agreement.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Permits grants to the advising organization from a DAF when it is §170(b)(1)(A).
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Statute §4958(c)(2) treats grants to a donor/donor-advisor as excess benefit; the proposed rule avoids this only by treating such funds as non-DAFs.

landscape_update_candidates: Fidelity Charitable bars 501(c)(3) organizations as account holders.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Which service charges may be charged to DAF funds, on what cost basis and with what disclosure (and is a recovery ceiling appropriate)?
original_provisional_answer: Special-request service charges to DAF funds are permitted only when (a) listed in the fee schedule disclosed before the request, (b) the donor affirms the charge, and (c) the charge is cost-based. The annual cost-recovery ratio per charge must not exceed 1.10; above that the price is reduced at the next schedule version.

Payments from a DAF to donors/advisors are automatic excess benefits.
Market: Fidelity Charitable charges administrative fees, allocates contribution/selling costs and program-specific fees to giving accounts, disclosed in program guidelines.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Fees and Expenses; Costs associated with contributions

authoritative_findings.claim: State fiduciary cost standard: costs must be appropriate and reasonable (UPMIFA §3(c)(1)/UPIA).

supporting_interpretation: Fund-specific service charges are permissible if reasonable, disclosed, and not paid to donors/advisors or related persons; cost basis is good evidence of reasonableness. The 1.10 ratio is a business control, not a legal limit.
competing_interpretation: Some argue any charge above cost is a profit on charitable assets; others note sponsors' overall fee schedules are not cost-based and are lawful if reasonable.
applicability_to_unbound: Fee schedule versioning and payee screening.
business_assumptions: Grade-B cost data ±15%
recommended_answer: Confirm with corrections: service charges are allowed when listed in the disclosed schedule, reasonable (cost-based is the evidence), and never paid directly or indirectly to a donor, advisor, family member or 35% entity. Donor affirmation is a good practice, not a legal requirement. Keep 1.10 as a review trigger (not a legal safe harbor, and not a service denial).

consequences_if_wrong: Unreasonable fund-specific fee could be a deemed (taxable) distribution under the proposed rule; state AG scrutiny.
conservative_fallback: No special service charges in R1 (current R1 scope).
alternative_design: Fold special-service costs into the uniform administrative fee: lowest legal exposure (uniform fees generally reasonable), but cross-subsidizes heavy users.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a service charge whose payee is a related party of the fund's donor/advisor, When posted, Then it is blocked.
Given a charge not in the schedule version disclosed before the request, When posted, Then it is rejected.
Given annual recovery ratio >1.10, When the report runs, Then a pricing review item is created.
external_authorization_required: Sponsor-approved fee schedule (board or delegated finance committee) disclosed in program guidelines.

related_question_answers.answer: Use the 1.10 ratio as a review trigger, calibrated by class and cost basis; no legal source sets a ceiling.
1.5 has no legal basis; treat as a scenario parameter. Legal test is reasonableness and no payment to donor-related persons.

authoritative_findings.claim: Sponsor has exclusive legal control over DAF assets; donors hold advisory privileges only.

No statute or regulation requires a sponsor to make, or forbids it from holding, a grant to an eligible recipient; distributions to §170(b)(1)(A) organizations are excepted from §4966 tax regardless of allegations.
No federal source sets a maximum review period for discretionary holds.

supporting_interpretation: No law fixes criteria or duration; board policy controls.
competing_interpretation: Narrow criteria reduce perceived arbitrariness; broader criteria match market practice.
applicability_to_unbound: Platform enforces whatever criteria and maxima the board approves.
business_assumptions: Sponsor board approves policy annually
recommended_answer: Board-approved criteria: adjudicated findings, regulator actions, and official pending matters (indictment, AG or IRS action, government investigation the sponsor is informed of); media allegations only with elevated approval. Maximum review period 90 days, renewable once per new evidence, with automatic release. These are policy choices, not legal requirements.
remaining_uncertainty: Board preference.
consequences_if_wrong: Donor relations; no tax consequence.
alternative_design: Redirect offer instead of hold.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a hold with evidence class not listed in the approved policy, When submitted, Then it is rejected.

related_question_answers.answer: Indictment-triggered holds may be permitted under board policy.

exact_question: Does §4967 apply if a broad geographic class happens to include the donor's grandchildren?
original_provisional_answer: (No answer recorded.) Requirement: BenefitAndPurposeGate rejects classes defined by reference to the donor's or advisor's family; class disabled by default. The RecipientClass rule MUST include a class 'Section530AGeneralFundingContribution', disabled by default per sponsor, mapping to Permitted only when: a Treasury acceptance agreement reference identifying the sponsor as eligible donor is recorded; the qualified or approved class definition is record

authoritative_findings.claim: A DAF-funded §530A general funding contribution is not a distribution to a natural person under §4966 and is treated as exercising ER; classes are broad and defined by objective criteria (geography, birth year).
The temporary regulations do not address §4967 or §4958.
§4967 applies to more-than-incidental benefits to §4958(f)(7) persons, which include family members; family includes grandchildren (and siblings under §4958(f)(4)).
PF analogue: a disqualified person's incidental or tenuous benefit as a member of the public or of a qualifying objective program is not self-dealing.

supporting_interpretation: A grandchild who receives an allocation only as one member of a broad, objectively defined class (e.g., all children born in a county in a year) receives an incidental benefit by analogy to §53.4941(d)-2(f)(2); §4967 should not apply. The analysis changes if the class is small or chosen so relatives make up a meaningful share, or the donor shaped the class.
competing_interpretation: §4967 has no regulations; the IRS could view any donor-advised payment whose recipients include relatives as more than incidental, especially if the donor selected the geography.
applicability_to_unbound: Gate should compute class size and whether the donor recommended the class definition.
business_assumptions: Class disabled in R1 (XID-NPG-003)
recommended_answer: Likely no §4967 tax where the class is the Treasury-accepted broad class and relatives benefit only as members (reasoned by PF incidental-benefit analogy). Gate: reject classes defined by family; route to review classes below a sponsor-set size threshold or where the donor proposed the class boundaries. Class stays disabled in R1.
remaining_uncertainty: No §4967 regulations; temp regs silent; small-class cases untested.
consequences_if_wrong: 125% of the benefit on advisor/recipient; 10% on knowing managers.
alternative_design: Sponsor-initiated (not donor-advised) general funding contributions from sponsor unrestricted funds avoid §4967 advisor element.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a class definition referencing the donor's family, Then Reject.
Given a class below the size threshold, Then SponsorReview.
external_authorization_required: Treasury acceptance agreement naming the sponsor as eligible donor (per temp regs) before enabling.
landscape_update_candidates: TD 10056 (2026-09-30) treats DAF-funded Trump-account general funding contributions as non-natural-person distributions with deemed ER, expiring 2029-09-30.

authoritative_findings.claim: Even when no ER is needed, §4967 (more-than-incidental benefit) and §4958(c)(2) (payments to donor-related persons) still apply.
Notice 2017-73 identifies event tickets/participation and pledges as benefit risk areas.
Supporting organizations are excepted only if not disqualified (donor control of a supported organization).
Proposed anti-abuse rule for plans routed through intermediaries; deemed distributions for uses conferring more-than-incidental benefit.
TEOS reliance is lost where the grantor is responsible for or aware of the change in status (e.g., grants large enough to tip public support).

supporting_interpretation: Tier 2 is a business control; authority identifies where non-ER grants still carry excise-tax risk.
competing_interpretation: More Tier-2 cases increase cost; sponsors may accept certifications instead.
applicability_to_unbound: Deterministic triggers.
business_assumptions: Tier 2 = written terms plus reviewer
recommended_answer: Put in Tier 2 (non-ER) grants with any of: (1) donor/advisor/family affiliation with the recipient or benefit signals (events, memberships, tuition, naming beyond recognition, pledges outside sponsor policy); (2) Type I/II supporting organizations; (3) fiscally sponsored projects that are separate entities; (4) intermediaries with a stated program/country preference; (5) ED-based foreign recipients; (6) governmental units; (7) grant amount large relative to recipient revenue (public-support tipping); (8) restricted or conditional grants (challenge, matching, multi-year). Counsel can trim the list; none is legally mandated.
remaining_uncertainty: Sponsor's review capacity and risk appetite.
consequences_if_wrong: Missed benefit-risk grants (125%/10% §4967; §4958 full amount).
alternative_design: Donor certification at recommendation time for benefit questions with sampling review.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a recommendation with a declared donor affiliation to the recipient, Then GrantTermsTier = 2.
Given a grant >X% of recipient's latest reported revenue, Then Tier 2.

exact_question: When complex-asset processing is outsourced, may the vendor fee be charged to the fund, and is that a saving?
original_provisional_answer: Recommendation: Charge to fund only as a disclosed, donor-affirmed, cost-based service charge; never report the bearer shift as an operating saving.
jurisdiction: US federal; sponsor state fiduciary law

authoritative_findings.claim: Proposed rule: reasonable grant-related/investment fees are not distributions; fund-specific expenses may be reasonable; fund-specific expenses paid to donor/advisor/related persons are deemed distributions.
Market: Fidelity Charitable allocates costs of reviewing, receiving, holding and selling contributed property to the giving account and credits net proceeds.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Costs associated with contributions; Contribution processing

authoritative_findings.claim: Payments to donor-related persons from a DAF are automatic excess benefits.

supporting_interpretation: Charging an outsourced complex-asset vendor's reasonable fee to the fund (net-proceeds treatment) is consistent with market practice and the proposed reasonableness standard, if disclosed and the vendor is not donor-related. It is a change in who bears cost, not an operating saving.
competing_interpretation: If the sponsor previously absorbed these costs in its uniform fee, shifting them reduces charitable assets of affected funds; disclosure and reasonableness matter.
applicability_to_unbound: Economic reporting must not count bearer shift as saving.
business_assumptions: Vendor fee is arm's-length
recommended_answer: Yes, the vendor fee may be charged to the fund as a disclosed, reasonable (cost-based) contribution cost, netted from proceeds, provided the vendor is not the donor, advisor, family member or 35% entity. It is not an operating saving; report it as a bearer shift.
remaining_uncertainty: Final rule wording; state cost standard text unverified.
consequences_if_wrong: Unreasonable fee: deemed distribution (proposed); state AG scrutiny.
alternative_design: Charge via uniform complex-asset program fee schedule.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a vendor related to the donor, When fee is charged to the fund, Then blocked.
Given economics report, Then vendor fees charged to funds are excluded from operating savings.
external_authorization_required: Sponsor fee schedule disclosure in program guidelines.

exact_question: Defer 50-state charity registration/standing acquisition and state-rule tracking until a decision consumes them?
original_provisional_answer: Recommendation: Defer; grantee state standing is not a grantor obligation (XRA-015) and was rejected as a gate (XRJ-NPG-002).
jurisdiction: US federal; California; other states (not surveyed)

authoritative_findings.claim: Federal §4966 exception and TEOS reliance turn on federal classification, not state registration.

California: an organization not in good standing with the Registry (delinquent, suspended, revoked) may not operate or solicit donations in California, including through charitable fundraising platforms.
California charitable fundraising platform rules require platforms that list/recommend charities by name or provide giving software to confirm IRS, FTB and AG good standing for each recipient.
Reported: delinquent or suspended registrants may not disburse charitable funds (11 CCR §999.9.4).
Market: Fidelity Charitable requires Eligible Grant Recipients to be 'in good standing under both applicable federal and state laws'.

supporting_interpretation: For most states, grantee registration status is not a grantor obligation, so deferring a 50-state build is reasonable. California is an exception worth handling now: its AG registry and CFP rules may reach platforms that list or recommend charities, and Unbound's donor-facing search could be within 'Type A' or 'Type E' activity.
competing_interpretation: DAF grantmaking by a sponsor is not solicitation, so CFP rules may not apply; coverage of DAF platforms is not addressed in the sources found.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound as a software platform may itself be a CFP if it lists charities to California donors; requires a scoped check.
business_assumptions: Some sponsors serve California donors
recommended_answer: Defer the 50-state build, but do not defer California: ingest the California AG Registry status (and FTB/IRS status) as a recipient attribute, display it, and let sponsor policy choose hold versus warn. Also determine whether Unbound's charity search/recommendation features make it a California charitable fundraising platform. The claim that state standing is never a grantor concern should be narrowed.
remaining_uncertainty: Whether CFP rules reach DAF sponsor platforms; exact §999.9.4 text unverified; other states not surveyed.
consequences_if_wrong: California AG enforcement against a platform; grants to delinquent charities that cannot lawfully operate in California.
conservative_fallback: California status check as warning for all sponsors.
alternative_design: Do not list or recommend charities to donors (search only by EIN entered by donor): reduces CFP exposure; loses discovery value.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a recipient registered in California with status Delinquent/Suspended/Revoked, When a grant is evaluated, Then the status is shown and the sponsor-configured action (hold or warn) applies.
reconsideration_triggers: CA AG guidance on DAF sponsors and CFPs

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: States grantee state standing is not a grantor obligation.
corrections_to_prior_records.correction: True under federal tax law, but California registry and CFP rules restrict operation/soliciting by non-good-standing charities and may impose verification on platforms; market leader requires state good standing.

landscape_update_candidates: Fidelity Charitable requires state good standing; California CFP regime may affect DAF platforms.
